title: Mini-Whiteboards Work. Participation Is the Point.
author: Andrew Watson
summary: Andrew Watson reviews what he describes as the first meta-analysis he has seen on mini-whiteboards, Robbie Marsh and colleagues' updated review of response card research. Across 29 studies, compared with hand-raising, whiteboards and response cards raised participation by almost 60 percent, cut off-task behavior by more than 25 percent, and lifted quiz and test scores by 18 and nearly 14 percent, with academic gains larger in special education settings and behavioral gains larger in general education. Watson then tempers the enthusiasm with two statistical cautions: the studies averaged only about 15 participants each, and heterogeneity was extremely high, so effects varied widely for reasons the data cannot explain. His third and main point is conceptual: the benefit comes from having every student respond frequently during instruction, not from the whiteboard itself. He therefore reframes the takeaway as moving away from hand-raising toward routines such as turn-and-talks, cold calling, clickers and do-nows that keep everyone responding, with mini-whiteboards as one good option among many.
points: The Marsh meta-analysis found participation almost 60 percent higher and off-task behavior more than 25 percent lower than in hand-raising classes.
Watson flags that 29 studies covered only 405 students, an average sample of about 15, which limits confidence.
Heterogeneity statistics of 98 to 99 percent mean results ranged from large to negligible, so individual classrooms may see very different effects.
His practical conclusion is to abandon hand-raising in favor of any all-respond routine, of which mini-whiteboards are only one.
quotes: Today, for the first time, I came across a meta-analysis looking at research into the topic. Its conclusions – and limitations – make for helpful reading.
Participation was almost 60% higher in the MWB class. Off-task behavior fell by more than 25% (or, on-task behavior rose by more than 25%)
More precisely: students in special education settings saw higher academic gains. Those in general education classes saw more behavioral improvement.
You might have noticed that the 29 studies included 405 people. In other words, the average sample size in each study was 15. That’s TINY.
We don’t have enough data to know why they helped a lot in some cases and only a little in others. Simply put: your mileage may vary.
Mini-whiteboards do — but not because they’re special. They work because they make it easy to get everyone responding, all at once. And they’re not the only way to do that.
Move away from hand-raising and toward routines that keep everyone responding. Once teachers make that shift, MWBs are one good option among many — not the only answer.
